knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      warning = FALSE, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5,
                      fig.align = "center", dpi = 96, fig.retina = 1, dev = "png", out.width = "100%")

knitr::include_graphics(if (file.exists("casimir-landing.svg")) "casimir-landing.svg" else
  system.file("app", "www", "casimir-landing.svg", package = "casimir"))

This walkthrough designs a catch survey on Island X, rolls it, raises it to
catch per species and fleet segment, and then judges the design by spinning
it many times and running it for five years. Every step is a plain function;
the app (`run_app()`) calls the same ones.

# 1. Build the island

```{r island}
library(casimir)
fish <- cas_fishery(island_x(), seed = 1)
fish
```

Ten years are simulated: five years of burn-in, in which stocks respond to
fishing and boats enter and leave, then a five-year sampling programme.

```{r map, fig.height = 6.5}
plot(fish)
```

Where the fish live, where each segment fishes, and where the catch comes
from:

```{r maps-species, fig.height = 5.2}
plot_species_map(fish)
```

```{r maps-effort, fig.height = 4}
plot_effort_map(fish, by = "segment")
```

```{r maps-catch, fig.height = 7.5}
plot_catch_map(fish, species = c("Scomber colias", "Thunnus alalunga", "Merluccius merluccius"),
               by = "segment")
```

::: {.info}
**The population.** `fish$landings` holds every trip: site, date, segment,
hours fished, landing hour and the true landed weight of each species. This
census is the answer key: no real survey has one.
:::

```{r truth}
year <- max(fish$years)
truth <- cas_truth(fish, years = year, by = c("year", "segment"))
xtabs(round(kg / 1000, 1) ~ species + segment, truth)
```

# 2. The frame survey

What the planner knows: boats by site and segment, and fishing days.

```{r frame}
frame <- frame_survey(fish)
frame
```

# 3. Design and betting slip

Six site-days per site type and quarter, three landings per segment at each
visit, a 10 kg basket from each.

```{r design}
d <- cas_design(m = 6, n = 3, w_kg = 10, name = "A")
d
design_cost(d, fishery = fish)   # enumerator-hours per year
```

::: {.predict}
**Betting slip.** Before rolling: what CV do you expect for *Scomber
colias*, the main species? And for *Dentex dentex*, the rarest?
:::

# 4. Roll

```{r roll}
s <- draw_sample(fish, d, year = year, seed = 2)
s
head(s$A, 6)   # Form A: landings counted at each visit, by segment
head(s$B, 6)   # Form B: sampled landings (W landed, w basket)
head(s$C, 6)   # Form C: species weights in the basket
```

The week x site grid of the training deck, for one stratum:

```{r grid, fig.height = 5.5, out.width = "70%"}
plot_design_grid(s, "Beach", quarter = 1)
```

How much of the fishery the sample saw, stage by stage:

```{r funnel, fig.height = 2.8}
plot_funnel(s, fish)
```

And where the sampled boats had been fishing:

```{r sample-map, fig.height = 6.5}
plot_sample_map(s, fish)
```

# 5. Raise

```{r raise}
e <- estimate_catch(s)
e
```

Each step is kept: `e$landing` (basket to landing), `e$psu` (landings to the
site-day), `e$stratum` (site-days to the stratum).

```{r estimate-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot_estimate(e, fish)
```

**By fleet segment.** Each segment is raised in its own strata, so catch by
species and segment comes straight out:

```{r by-segment, fig.height = 5}
plot_catch_by(e, by = "segment", fishery = fish)
head(catch_by(e, by = "segment", fishery = fish))
```

Blocks can be any combination of segment, site type and quarter:

```{r by-site-segment, fig.height = 7}
plot_catch_by(e, by = c("site_type", "segment"), fishery = fish,
              species = c("Scomber colias", "Thunnus alalunga", "Merluccius merluccius",
                          "Pagellus erythrinus"))
```

::: {.info}
**Small cells.** A species that a segment lands rarely is often missed
entirely: an estimate of zero with no interval. Totals are more reliable than
their parts.
:::

# 6. Spin: is the design any good?

One sample is one estimate. Spinning repeats the whole survey on the same
island; here design A against design B, which costs about the same but
visits more site-days (8 per stratum) and samples one landing per segment.

```{r spin, fig.height = 7}
ev_a <- replicate_design(fish, d, R = 200, seed = 3)
ev_b <- replicate_design(fish, cas_design(m = 8, n = 1, w_kg = 10, name = "B"), R = 200, seed = 3)
c(A = ev_a$cost, B = ev_b$cost)
plot_spin(list(A = ev_a, B = ev_b))
```

```{r spin-table, fig.height = 4.5}
plot_eval(rbind(data.frame(design = "A", ev_a$summary),
                data.frame(design = "B", ev_b$summary)))
```

::: {.info}
**Reading the spin.** The boxes sit on the truth: the estimators are
unbiased. The spread is the precision: narrow for the main species, wide for
the rare ones. At about the same cost, design A is more precise for every
species: on Island X the landings of one day differ a lot (different boats,
tactics and grounds), so sampling three of them per visit pays more than
visiting more site-days.
:::

# 7. A five-year programme

The same design in each of the last five years. With `frame = "first"`, the
frame survey of the first year is used throughout.

```{r series, fig.height = 5.5}
sv <- run_survey(fish, d, frame = "first", seed = 4)
plot_series(sv, fish)
```

By segment, for three species:

```{r series-segment, fig.height = 7}
plot_series(sv, fish, by = "segment",
            species = c("Scomber colias", "Thunnus alalunga", "Merluccius merluccius"))
```

# 8. Plant a problem

The trainer switches on a field problem; the trainee looks for its
signature. Here the enumerator leaves at 13:00.

```{r artefact, fig.height = 7}
ev_sw <- replicate_design(fish, d, R = 200, seed = 3, artefacts = artefacts(short_watch = 13))
plot_spin(list(A = ev_a, `A, short watch` = ev_sw))
```

::: {.flag}
**Warning flag.** Long trips land late: the offshore species of the large
motor boats almost vanish, while coastal canoe species lose a third. A
segment common in the frame but rare in Form A points to the watch hours.
:::

# 9. Cash out

```{r cashout, eval = FALSE}
export_survey(s, dir = "survey_A")                          # for trainees
export_survey(s, dir = "survey_A_key", answer_key = fish)   # with the answer key
```
